itineraries.title: Extended Cappadocia in 8 Days: Kayseri, Göreme, Konya
itineraries.subtitle: Traverse Cappadocia over 8 days, from the fairy chimneys of Göreme to the whirling dervishes of Konya.
itineraries.notes: Hot-air balloon flights depend on weather; plan for 2 nights in Göreme to give yourself a second chance. Lake Tuz is best visited between April and June for flamingos or July-August for the salt.
itineraries.climate: Best time: April-June and September-October, temperatures 15-25°C, clear skies perfect for hot air balloons. Avoid July-August (scorching heat 30-35°C, dust) and December-February (freezing nights, possible snow). High altitude (1200 m) means cool nights even in summer.

visits.text: Mount Erciyes towers over Kayseri at 3,916 m, the highest peak in Central Anatolia. This extinct stratovolcano shaped all of Cappadocia with its eruptions. The ski resort lies 40 minutes from downtown, the KAY airport 25 minutes. Skip high summer for skiing: the resort typically opens November to May.

Built from black basalt, Kayseri's citadel dates to the 3rd century, remodeled in the 15th by the Ottomans. It has morphed into a covered bazaar where they sell local sucuk sausages and pastırma cured beef. Budget an hour for the circuit, free entry. The vibe stays very local, barely touristic for a city of 1.4 million.

Hunat Hatun remains one of Turkey's finest Seljuk complexes. Mosque, madrasa, mausoleum and hammam, all built in 1238 by order of Queen Mahperi Hunat, wife of Keykubad I. The stonework is sober, the carvings delicate. Free entry, bring a headscarf and covered clothing for the mosque still in active use.

activities.text: Try the mantı kayserili, meat-filled dumplings drowned in a sauce of yogurt, garlic and paprika-infused butter. This is the city's absolute specialty, served everywhere. Portions are small, count on two plates. A good restaurant: Elmacıoğlu İskender, near Cumhuriyet Square. Avoid tourist chains near the castle.

practical_info.tip: Good mantı shows in the size of the dumpling, no bigger than a fingernail.

activities.text: If you come in winter, count on 40 minutes by car to Erciyes ski resort. A day pass runs around 800 TL in high season. The red run from the Hisarcık summit offers the best view. In summer, the cable car also operates for hiking toward the crater, 350 TL round-trip.

practical_info.tip: Check lift operation the day before—frequent closures in high wind.

visits.text: Touristy as hell, the Göreme Open Air Museum earns its reputation: arrive at 8 AM sharp when the gate opens. You'll have the churches to yourself thirty minutes before the tour buses roll in. The complex counts about a dozen chapels carved from tuff, dated 10th to 13th century. Budget two hours minimum.

Listed as UNESCO in 1985, the entire Göreme National Park holds some of the world's best-preserved Byzantine frescoes. The Dark Church (Karanlık Kilise) remains the centerpiece, with a separate ticket. Its darkness saved the pigments, restored after fourteen years of cleaning pigeon droppings. 100 TL on top of the museum ticket.

The smell of damp tuff and wax hits you in Tokalı Chapel, the largest at Göreme, just outside the museum. It's free, often overlooked by tour groups. The 9th-century frescoes narrate the 12 apostles in red-and-blue comic strips. Low ceiling, expect to duck. Budget 30 minutes.

activities.text: Walk Pigeon Valley to Uçhisar, about 1h30 on a marked trail along the cliff. The pigeon houses carved in the tuff give the valley its name: locals collected guano as fertilizer for the vineyards. Hiking shoes mandatory, bring water. Start early, the trail is exposed.

practical_info.tip: The return to Göreme is either on foot via Love Valley or by taxi (200 TL).

activities.text: Cappadocians call the chimneys peri bacaları, literally fairy chimneys. Head to Zelve, calmer than Göreme, to see the densest cluster: three valleys hollowed with troglodyte dwellings occupied until 1952. Budget 2 hours, 8 km from Göreme. Entry ticket 200 TL in 2026.

practical_info.tip: Morning is better for light in the chapels.

visits.text: Çavuşin beats its reputation as a mere stopover village. The abandoned old village crumbles into the cliff, its troglodyte houses visible from the road. The great Church of St. John the Baptist, cut into the rockface, is one of Cappadocia's oldest. Free access, but climbing required to reach the nave. No guard, use caution.

Pink climbs at sunrise over Red Valley, blended with orange and yellow. This palette gave the valley its name. Trails wind between pinnacles and pass several low-key chapels. The Red Valley café-garden, at the high point, serves tea with a view of the hot-air balloons. Open from 5 AM in season.

Dated 964-965, the Church of Nicephorus Phocas, Çavuşin's second church on the opposite slope, holds remarkably preserved Byzantine frescoes with a rare portrait of the emperor. More discreet than St. John the Baptist, it's watched by a neighbor who opens on request. Paid entry at the base, count on 100 TL. Access via fragile exterior staircase, use caution.

activities.text: Book your hot-air balloon flight at least three nights ahead, more in high season. Takeoff is at 5 AM, hotel transfer included. Count on €150 to €250 depending on standard and duration (45-90 min). Over 100 balloons launch on favorable mornings. If the flight is cancelled for wind, you're refunded or rescheduled.

practical_info.tip: Dress warm even in summer: it's 10°C colder at altitude.

activities.text: If you like pottery, push to Avanos on the banks of the Kızılırmak, 10 km north of Göreme. The pottery tradition goes back to the Hittites, the red clay comes from the river. Workshops like Chez Galip or Sezai Baykan do demonstrations. You can try the wheel, about 30 minutes for 200 TL.

practical_info.tip: Buy early in the visit, more room for negotiation.

visits.text: Rising 60 m high, Uçhisar Castle is actually a giant fairy chimney hollowed with tunnels, stairs and rooms. It's Cappadocia's highest point, used as a watchtower since the Hittites. The steep climb is on foot. The summit opens a 360° view over all the valleys. Ticket 150 TL in 2026.

Uçhisar beats Göreme for spending the night: quieter, higher, with the region's best cave hotels. The village climbs around the castle, its cobbled lanes preserved. Several café-terraces overlook Pigeon Valley. It's the right spot for sunset over the tethered balloons and the valley below.

activities.text: Climb in late afternoon to the summit of Uçhisar Castle for sunset. The stone heats then turns pink-violet, panoramic view of Erciyes in the background. Avoid weekends, the summit fills fast after 5 PM. Cap and closed shoes essential, lots of steep stairs inside.

practical_info.tip: Last summit access is usually 30 minutes before official sunset.

visits.text: Under a plain street, eight levels carved in tuff descend to 85 m depth at Derinkuyu, Cappadocia's deepest known underground city. It could shelter up to 20,000 people with livestock and provisions for months. Narrow tunnels, ceiling height often under 1.70 m. Claustrophobes stay away.

Probably dating to the 8th-7th century BC in the Phrygian era, Derinkuyu was mainly used from the 2nd century by Christians fleeing Roman persecutions, then in Byzantine and Seljuk periods. Rediscovered by accident in 1963 during a cellar renovation. Less than 10% of the complex has been explored.

activities.text: Visit Kaymaklı as a complement, 10 km north of Derinkuyu: it's the second accessible underground city, wider and shallower, with more airy galleries than its cousin. Four levels open to the public. Both can be done in the same half-day, count on 6 hours with the road. Combined ticket sometimes available.

practical_info.tip: Prefer Kaymaklı if you're claustrophobic, passages are wider than at Derinkuyu.

visits.text: Locals talk about the Virgin's smile at Eski Gümüşler, a Byzantine rock monastery 10 km from Niğde. The fresco depicts a Theotokos (Mother of God) with a half-smile, which would make it one of the rare examples in the world. Rediscovered in 1962, restored by a British team. Entry about 100 TL, open daily except Monday.

Built in 1223 by Governor Beşare for Seljuk Sultan Keykubad I, Niğde's Alaaddin Mosque stands on the citadel hill. Three domes, massive minaret, carved door depicting at certain sun hours the shadow of a crowned woman's head. Free visit, headscarf provided at entrance.

activities.text: Eat a kayseri mantısı in downtown Niğde before hitting the road again. The town is mainly agricultural, not touristic, the lokantas serve simple and hearty cuisine. Thursday's market runs around the clock tower, good chance to catch local life. Count on 100 to 150 TL for a full meal.

practical_info.tip: Thursday is market day, outside tourist season expect big crowds.

visits.text: The shade of poplars drops the temperature several degrees as you descend the 400 steps into Ihlara Valley. The contrast with the steppe is striking: here water flows, orchards green, village women still wash their laundry in the Melendiz. The valley runs 14 km, count on 3 to 4 hours for the central section.

Stretching 14 km, Ihlara Valley shelters nearly sixty Byzantine rock churches from the 11th-13th centuries. About a dozen can be visited along the way. The finest frescoes are at Sümbüllü Kilise (Church of the Hyacinths) and Yılanlı Kilise (Church of the Serpents). Single entry ticket at the south entrance, 100 TL in 2026.

activities.text: Descend the 400 steps at the south entrance near Ihlara village, walk 3.5 km to Belisırma where floating restaurants serve trout and köfte on platforms above the river. You can go back by taxi (200 TL for 5 km) or continue 4 km to Selime Monastery. Count on 7-8h for the full route.

practical_info.tip: Avoid July-August, heat in the canyon exceeds 35°C.

visits.text: Helvadere isn't a destination per se, more the starting point for Mount Hasan and a photo stop on the steppe. The Seljuk village, modest, keeps a few stone mosques. 30 km south of Aksaray, it's the outpost for hikers aiming for the volcano's summit. A mountain lodge hosts trekkers.

Peaking at 3,268 m, Hasan Dağı is an imposing twin-peaked stratovolcano whose last eruption dates to about 6200 BC. This eruption would be depicted in a Neolithic fresco at Çatalhöyük, considered the first map or landscape of humanity.

activities.text: If you're an experienced hiker, count on 6 hours of walking one-way from the car-accessible refuge to reach the summit of Hasan Dağı. Trail marked in summer, but mountaineering gear required in winter. Aksaray's mountaineering festival runs every July. Otherwise, from Helvadere the view of the volcano is plenty.

practical_info.tip: For the summit hike, leave Helvadere at 5 AM, fog rises fast after 10.

visits.text: Salt crunches underfoot, like snow, on the southeast shore of Lake Tuz near Şereflikoçhisar. The surface forms a perfect mirror early in the season, a blinding white crust in July-August. Sunglasses mandatory, extra sunscreen. Access is from a free parking lot then 200 m on foot across the salt.

Turkey's second-largest lake, Tuz Gölü is also one of the world's saltiest, average depth about 50 cm. It hosts a major breeding colony of flamingos, one of the most active in the region. The lake also supplies a large share of Turkey's salt.

activities.text: Go to the south shore between April and June for flamingos, May-June for chicks, July-August for salt crust and algae that pink the water. The south shore near Şereflikoçhisar concentrates the best photo spots and a café-restaurant. Avoid the lake edge after rain, the salt turns muddy.

practical_info.tip: Bring your binoculars, flamingos nest 1-2 km from shore, out of reach without optics.

visits.text: Built in 1274 over Rumi's tomb (Mevlana), Konya's mausoleum is the spiritual heart of world Sufism. The Persian poet and theologian rests there under a draped sarcophagus, topped with a green turban. The turquoise conical roof has become Konya's symbol. Free entry. Covered clothing required, no photos inside.

Incense and cedar wood still float in the old dervish dormitories, transformed into exhibition halls of the Mevlana Museum. You'll see the white robes, conical felt hats (sikke), manuscripts of Rumi's Mathnawi calligraphed by hand. The central garden fountain refreshes from the entrance.

Karatay Museum merits the detour just for its dome: completed in 1251 as a Seljuk madrasa, it now houses an exceptional collection of ceramics and turquoise tiles. The dome is carpeted with stars of black, blue and turquoise ceramic. Entry 100 TL in 2026. 200 m from Mevlana Museum.

activities.text: Eat an etli ekmek in a downtown Konya lokanta. It's the city's signature dish: a flat, thin and crispy dough, covered with spiced minced meat, sometimes 60 cm long. Mehmet Dede Etli Ekmek restaurant, near Mevlana Museum, makes the classic version. Count on 200 TL for two.

practical_info.tip: Etli ekmek is eaten with your hands, folded in half like a wrap.

activities.text: If you come on a Saturday evening, book your seat for the sema ceremony at the Mevlana Cultural Center. The whirling dervishes perform their hour-long ritual, slow and symbolic rotation. Show free in theory, sometimes 50-100 TL in season. No applause during the ceremony: it's a religious act, not a performance.

practical_info.tip: Arrive 45 minutes early, seats sell out in high season.

visits.text: Completed around 1220, Konya's Alaaddin Mosque crowns the hill of the same name in the heart of the old town. It's one of Turkey's oldest mosques, founded by the Seljuks. Built on the ruins of a Byzantine church, it reuses its Corinthian columns. Free visit, headscarf and covered clothing mandatory.

The silence in the forest of columns surprises upon entering Alaaddin Mosque. Forty-two reused ancient columns support a flat wooden ceiling, no main dome. At the foot of the hill, Alaaddin public park offers one of the few shaded green spaces downtown. Fountain and benches, ideal for a breather.

İnce Minare disappoints those expecting too much: its famous double minaret was struck by lightning in 1901, only a stump remains. But the carved 1264 portal remains one of Seljuk Gothic's masterpieces. Inside, a small museum of stone sculpture. 100 TL in 2026, 30 minutes is enough.

activities.text: Stroll through Konya's covered bazaar: saffron and sumac spices, rose and burnt sugar candies, cotton fabrics, Anatolian white fir for handicrafts. Less touristic than Istanbul's Grand Bazaar, much more authentic. Spot the workshops of copper and traditional felt (keçe). Count on 1h30 for the full tour.

practical_info.tip: Bargain systematically, it's expected in Konya's bazaar.

activities.text: Konyalı will tell you about tirit, an ancient dish of boiled lamb, placed on flatbread soaked in broth and topped with yogurt. Served at banquets for local festivals, rarer in restaurants. Hacı Şükrü, near Mevlana Museum, serves it daily at noon. Reserve or arrive before 12:30, it goes fast.

practical_info.tip: Ask to taste the bamya çorbası as a starter, okra and tomato soup.

seo.h1_title: Extended Cappadocia in 8 Days: Kayseri, Göreme, Konya
seo.intro_paragraph: 8 days to cross Cappadocia and Central Anatolia, from Kayseri at the foot of Mount Erciyes to Konya, city of the whirling dervishes. You'll explore UNESCO-listed Göreme's rock-cut churches, descend the eight levels of Derinkuyu's underground city, hike the verdant Ihlara Valley, and walk the salt crusts of Lake Tuz.
seo.seo_hook: Göreme's fairy chimneys, Derinkuyu's underground city, Ihlara Valley, Lake Tuz and Konya's dervishes: 8 days across extended Cappadocia.
featured_list: Kayseri: northern gateway, at the foot of 3,916-m Mount Erciyes
Göreme: UNESCO open-air museum and 11th-century Byzantine frescoes
Uçhisar: 60-m natural citadel, Cappadocia's highest point
Ihlara Valley: 14-km green canyon with Byzantine rock churches
Derinkuyu: 8 underground levels, 85 m depth
Lake Tuz: Turkey's 2nd lake, flamingo breeding colony
Konya: Rumi's mausoleum (1274) and whirling dervish sema ceremonies

places_taglines.TR::kayseri: Industrial hub beneath Erciyes volcano, Cappadocia's rugged northern gateway.
places_taglines.TR::goreme: Where fairy chimneys shelter Byzantine frescoes painted in darkness and prayer.
places_taglines.TR::uchisar: A honeycombed stone citadel rising sixty meters above the Anatolian plateau.
places_taglines.TR::ihlara: A fourteen-kilometer green gash through the steppe, carved by the Melendiz River.
places_taglines.TR::derinkuyu: Eight levels tunneling eighty-five meters beneath an ordinary street, shelter for twenty thousand souls.
places_taglines.TR::nigde: A Seljuk stopover where the Virgin smiles from monastery walls.
places_taglines.TR::helvadere: A quiet gateway to the twin-peaked stratovolcano painted in Neolithic memory.
places_taglines.TR::sereflikochisar: Where salt mirrors the sky and flamingos breed in one of Anatolia's great shallows.
places_taglines.TR::konya: City of Rumi, where dervishes whirl in prayer and Seljuk stone speaks of empire.

highlights: Göreme Open Air Museum, UNESCO since 1985: Byzantine rock-cut churches and 11th-century frescoes
Derinkuyu, eight-level underground city descending 85 m in depth
Lake Tuz, Turkey's second lake, Middle East's main flamingo breeding colony
Mevlana Mausoleum in Konya, built in 1274, heart of the Sufi order of whirling dervishes
Mount Hasan, 3,268-m stratovolcano visible as far as Çatalhöyük in Neolithic painting

itineraries.title: Turkish Mesopotamia: 11 Days from Gaziantep to the Tigris
itineraries.subtitle: Cross Southeast Anatolia in 11 days, from the baklava capital to the black ramparts of Diyarbakır.
itineraries.notes: Hot region: avoid July and August, when temperatures exceed 40°C in Şanlıurfa and Harran. Check Hasankeyf site access before departure, as lake levels vary.
itineraries.climate: Best time: April-May and October-November, temperatures 15-28°C, ideal for archaeological sites. Avoid July-August at all costs (extreme heat 38-45°C, scorching sun). Winter is cold and occasionally snowy (December-February), less suitable for touring.

visits.text: Gaziantep wears its baklava capital nickname lightly: it's also the capital of pistachios, isot pepper, eggplant kebab, and one of the densest cuisines in the world. UNESCO designated it a Creative City of Gastronomy in 2015, alongside Lyon and Parma. Start with the historic center, restored across 5.5 km around the castle. Skip the crowded noon terraces—locals eat earlier than you'd think.

At Bakırcılar Çarşısı, the hammering of copper has set the rhythm of the day for four centuries. Workshops line the cobbled alleys below the castle. You'll watch trays, teapots, and kebab skewers forged by hand right in front of you. Haggle without hesitation—it's expected. Best prices are in the morning, before tour buses arrive.

Built in the Bronze Age, Gaziantep Castle has dominated the old town from its hilltop perch. The February 2023 earthquake damaged it severely, and restoration is ongoing. You may not be able to climb inside, but the circuit around the base of the ramparts remains one of the finest viewpoints over the city. Check access on the day with the tourist office.

activities.text: Locals start their day with beyran: a lamb broth simmered all night, served with rice and plenty of chili. Try it at the Coppersmiths' Bazaar from 8am, in a nameless diner. This isn't a dish for delicate stomachs, but it's the essence of Antep cuisine.

practical_info.tip: Ask for "beyran çorbası"; expect around 100 TL per bowl depending on location.

activities.text: Push open the door of Zincirli Bedesten in late afternoon: this restored Ottoman covered market gathers spices, kutnu fabrics, and Antep pistachios under a timbered roof. It's less touristy than the copper bazaar, with a more mixed atmosphere. Look for isot, the local smoked pepper with its own protected geographical indication.

practical_info.tip: The bedesten closes around 7pm; stay for Tahmis Kahvesi next door.

visits.text: One mosaic steals the show from all the rest: the Gypsy Girl at the Zeugma Museum. In a dark room, only her eyes are lit, and they follow you. The rest of the museum is vast: 2,448 m² of Roman mosaics rescued from the Birecik dam, across three floors. Budget two full hours.

Opened in 2011, the Zeugma Museum protects floor mosaics from the Roman villas of the ancient city of Belkis-Zeugma, founded around 300 BC. Don't miss the Ocean and Tethys mosaic, or the bronze Mars. The twelve panels recovered in 2018 from Bowling Green University have finally rejoined the original work. Avoid weekends—it's overrun with school groups.

The smell of hot sugar and clarified butter draws you in from the entrance of the Baklava Museum, housed in a restored Ottoman mansion. The displays show the 40 layers of phyllo pastry, thin as a page, and the role of Antep pistachios in baklava Gaziantep, which has been EU-protected since 2013. Small museum, big technical lesson.

activities.text: If you love pastry, book two hours at İmam Çağdaş, operating since 1887. Order the fıstıklı baklava and katmer with creamy pistachio. Service is quick, no fuss. It's the local reference, cited in every guide and always packed with Antep residents. Skip the copycat terraces downtown—the real deal is here.

practical_info.tip: Katmer is only served in the morning—it's a traditional breakfast.

activities.text: Taste menengiç, the coffee made from roasted wild pistachios rather than coffee beans. Tahmis Kahvesi next to Zincirli Bedesten has served it since the 17th century. Paired with a bite of halva, it's sweet and earthy.

practical_info.tip: Ask for sade (no sugar) to taste the pure pistachio.

visits.text: Touristy but striking: only the minaret emerges from the waters of Halfeti since 2000, when the Birecik dam submerged 40% of the old village. The rest lies beneath the surface—mosque, stone houses, orchards. Halfeti joined the Cittaslow network in 2013. Skip the jet-skis that turn the experience into a theme park.

Grown only here, the black rose of Halfeti draws its color from a very particular microclimate along the Euphrates bank. The buds are almost black in spring, turning deep crimson as they mature. The gardens that still produce them can be visited near the old village. It's inspired several perfumes since the 2010s.

activities.text: Board a boat on the Euphrates for a 90-minute loop to Rumkale, an ancient Armenian fortress at the confluence with the Merzimen. Boats depart from the old village quay from 9am, without fixed schedule. Expect 100 to 150 TL per person. Choose a collective boat over a jet-ski: the silence of the river makes half the experience.

practical_info.tip: Rumkale is under restoration; you can no longer disembark, only observe from the boat.

visits.text: Locals simply call it Balıklıgöl, the pool of fish. Islamic legend places Abraham's miracle here: Nemrod threw him into a fire, which turned into water, and the wood into carp. The carp are protected, never fished. The site is free, very busy in late afternoon with local families. Avoid midday and the scorching sun.

Built in 1211 by the Ayyubids, the Halil-ur-Rahman Mosque borders directly onto the sacred pool. Its shaded courtyard is one of the few places in Şanlıurfa where you can breathe in summer. The square minaret recalls Syrian models. Cover your shoulders and legs before entering; scarves provided at the entrance for women.

The air smells of isot and rubbed copper in Kazaz Bedesten, a covered market built in 1562. It's the oldest bazaar in Şanlıurfa, dedicated to fabrics and traditional outfits. All around: Sipahi for Kurdish carpets, the coppersmiths' bazaar, the pepper market. Haggle—it's expected.

activities.text: If you climb to Urfa Castle in late afternoon, the view over the pool and old town is worth the effort. Legend has it that Nemrod catapulted Abraham from those two Corinthian columns you still see at the top. Count on 20 minutes' walk from Balıklıgöl. The stairs are steep, closed at 7pm in summer.

practical_info.tip: Bring water—there's no refreshment stand at the summit.

activities.text: Buy a packet of pellets to feed the sacred carp of Balıklıgöl, about 5 TL from vendors around the pool. The fish rush in a compact shoal. According to locals, spotting a white carp brings luck. Don't bring your own food—it's forbidden to preserve the carp population.

practical_info.tip: A gesture appreciated by Turkish Muslim families, but respectful of the sacred nature of the place.

visits.text: Older than Stonehenge by several millennia, the Göbekli Tepe site has been dated between 9600 and 8200 BC by UNESCO. It was built by hunter-gatherers, before the invention of agriculture. This overturns our understanding of the Neolithic: the sacred preceded sedentism, not the other way around. Less than 5% of the site has been excavated.

Inscribed on UNESCO in 2018, the Göbekli Tepe site features 5.5-meter T-shaped limestone pillars, carved with bas-relief sculptures: wild boars, foxes, vultures, scorpions. A protective hall covers the main enclosures. You walk around them on walkways, without being able to descend. Klaus Schmidt, the German archaeologist who revealed it all, died on site in 2014.

activities.text: Arrive before 9am to avoid Turkish tour groups coming by bus from Şanlıurfa. The visitor center opens at 8am; a 10-minute film explains the context before climbing to the site. You can cover everything in 1.5 hours. The midday sun is merciless—no shade on the hill. The French audio guide is recommended.

practical_info.tip: Combined Göbekli Tepe + Karahantepe ticket available at the visitor center.

visits.text: The Şanlıurfa Archaeology Museum is by far the most important in Anatolia for the Neolithic. Opened in its current building in 2015, it displays nearly 10,000 pieces: original T-pillars from Göbekli Tepe, Karahantepe sculptures, Amazons mosaics from Haleplibahçe. Budget two hours minimum. Closed Tuesday mornings.

Standing 1.80 meters tall, the Urfa Man dates from around 9000 BC and is believed to be the world's oldest life-size statue. Found in 1993 during construction work in Yeni Mahalle, it's limestone, with obsidian eyes. No mouth, which intrigues archaeologists. It has its own display case at the museum—don't miss it on arrival.

The Mevlid-i Halil cave smells of dampness and incense. Muslim tradition places Abraham's birth here. Now part of a mosque complex adjoining Balıklıgöl, the cave can be visited for free. Men and women enter separately. Cover your hair and shoulders. The atmosphere is that of an active sanctuary, not a museum.

activities.text: Dine at Cevahir Konukevi, a restored 19th-century caravanserai serving Urfa cuisine: hand-prepared çiğ köfte, thin lahmacun, ali nazik with smoked eggplant. The inner courtyard is cooled with misters in summer. Moderate prices, and it's one of the few places still serving mırra, strong Arabic coffee.

practical_info.tip: Book for evening—it's full from 7:30pm in high season.

activities.text: The Urfalis call their city the city of prophets: tradition holds that Job, Abraham, and Elijah all left their mark here. Stroll through the Eyyübiye district at sunrise, when worshippers arrive at Balıklıgöl and the heat hasn't yet crushed you. The golden light on the stone walls is worth the early wake-up.

practical_info.tip: Avoid Friday midday; collective prayer makes circulation difficult.

visits.text: The dry silence of the Harran plain strikes you first. 44 km southeast of Şanlıurfa, a few kilometers from the Syrian border, the village remains one of the oldest known inhabited sites, mentioned in Genesis as Abraham's stop on the way to Canaan. The local language is still Arabic for many inhabitants, alongside Turkish and Kurdish.

Built between 744 and 750 by Marwan II, the Ulu Cami of Harran is considered the oldest mosque in Anatolia. Only the square minaret remains—atypical in Turkey—along with arches and foundations. The site also included the first Islamic university. All around, ruins of baths and cisterns. Access is free, ruined but open.

activities.text: Enter a beehive house: 4 to 5 meters high, in mud brick without a single wooden beam, with conical domes that insulate against heat. The Harran Kültür Evi tourist complex recreates the traditional way of life. Hot drink and flatbread offered, but plan for a tip. Allow 30 minutes; the visit is brief.

practical_info.tip: Real inhabited beehive houses remain on the village outskirts; ask residents for permission to approach.

visits.text: Less known than Göbekli Tepe, Karahantepe is still worth the archaeological detour: it's a twin site, also dated around 9400 BC, part of the Taş Tepeler (stone hills) network. Excavations began in 2019 and are advancing quickly. You can watch the workers at work from the walkways.

Under the protective hall, the eleven anthropomorphic pillars of Karahantepe's central sanctuary surround a relief figure: a human face carved directly into the rock, which doesn't exist at Göbekli Tepe. The elliptical building measures 28 meters wide. Less than 5% of the site has been cleared. Everything is still fresh; the effect is striking.

activities.text: If you've seen both sites, return to the Şanlıurfa Archaeology Museum: major pieces from Göbekli Tepe and Karahantepe are displayed there, including a replica of Sanctuary D and carved human heads. It's more complete than an on-site audio guide, especially for understanding the iconography of the reliefs.

practical_info.tip: The museum and site sometimes have a combined ticket; ask at the ticket office.

visits.text: Viranşehir means "ruined city" in Turkish, a name that sums up its eventful history. It was Constantia under the Romans and Byzantines, Tella d'Mawzlat for the Syriacs. Rebuilt by Constantine I in the 4th century after destruction by the Persians, it was a strategic lock on the Byzantine frontier. Today it's a large Kurdish cotton town, more useful as a stopover than a destination.

The Han El-Burur, a medieval caravanserai noted near Viranşehir, testifies to the town's role on the old caravan routes. The remains are modest, accessible at the eastern exit of the town. Allow 20 minutes for a photo stop, no more. It's mainly an opportunity to break the long stretch between Şanlıurfa and Mardin without forcing the stage.

activities.text: Take a meal break in Viranşehir before tackling the stretch to Mardin. Several lokantas lined up on the main street serve pistachio kebab and local çiğ köfte. Expect around 150 TL for a full meal with ayran. Avoid prayer times on Friday; many shops close for 45 minutes.

practical_info.tip: Gas stations plentiful; fill up here before the long straight to Mardin.

visits.text: The honey-colored stone of Mardin heats in the sun and gives the old town its unique glow. Perched at 1,100 meters on a rocky spur, it dominates the Mesopotamian plain that unfolds toward Syria. The alleys climb and descend steeply, cobbled, sometimes in steps. Sandals not recommended; closed shoes essential.

Dating from 1385, the Zinciriye Medresesi (or Sultan Isa Medrese) remains one of the finest examples of Artuqid architecture in Mardin. Its carved portal, two ribbed domes, and inner courtyard deserve your time. The terrace roof overlooks the Mesopotamian plain, accessible via a discreet staircase on the west side.

The Church of the Forty Martyrs is worth the detour: it honors the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste, Roman soldiers executed in the 4th century for their Christian faith. Also known as Kırklar Kilisesi, it dates back to the 6th century and still hosts a weekly mass in Aramaic, the language spoken by Jesus. Inside, Byzantine icons and an ancient baptismal font. The local Syriac Orthodox community is a minority but vibrant.

activities.text: Have breakfast in a konak in the old town: local cheeses, black olives from Hatay, pistachio honey, flatbread with molasses, and dibek coffee pounded in a mortar. Several mansion-restaurants line up their tables on terraces overlooking the plain. Expect around 200 TL per person; better to book on weekends.

practical_info.tip: Skip the instant coffee offered as an option—the pounded dibek is what deserves the trip.

activities.text: If you like terraces, reach the Kasimiye Medresesi on foot from the lower old town, about 25 minutes downhill. The central basin represents the Sirat bridge of Islamic tradition. The accessible roof offers the view featured on all postcards. Go at sunset—it's free but monitored.

practical_info.tip: Return to the old town by taxi; the climb is tough.

visits.text: A Byzantine crypt beneath a Syriac monastery: the basement of Deyrulzafaran houses an ancient temple dedicated to the Mesopotamian sun god Shamash, older than the Christian building. The transition between the two cults is visible in the stone, without rupture. That's what makes the place so dense with history.

Founded in the 5th century, Deyrulzafaran stands about 6 km east of Mardin, on a site once devoted to sun worship. It served as the seat of the Syriac Orthodox patriarch from 1160 to 1932. The visit is guided, the tour lasts 30 minutes, departures every half hour. Visits are in groups, sometimes bilingual English.

activities.text: Allow 30 km to reach Dara, the ancient Byzantine city southeast of Mardin. Its vaulted underground cisterns, rock-cut necropolis carved into the limestone, and 6th-century fortifications are worth half a day. The site is free access, poorly signposted, few visitors. Bring a flashlight for the cisterns.

practical_info.tip: The road between Deyrulzafaran and Dara isn't obvious; GPS recommended.

visits.text: Midyat should be savored slowly, alley after alley. The old town of Eski Midyat features medieval Syriac mansions in golden stone, hidden inner courtyards, bell towers of still-active churches. The Tur Abdin region was inscribed on UNESCO's tentative list in 2021 for its medieval churches and monasteries.

Founded in 397, the Mor Gabriel Monastery is the world's oldest still-active Syriac Orthodox monastery. 20 km east of Midyat, it's home to around twenty monks and nuns. The liturgy is in Syriac, a language derived from Aramaic. Organized visits all day; plan for a donation at the exit.

At the Konukevi, the smell of old wood and cardamom mingles in the vaulted rooms of this large 19th-century Syriac house, now the official guesthouse. You can visit even if you're not staying overnight; the hall and courtyard are accessible. It's one of the symbols of Midyat's Syriac heritage, restored by the state.

activities.text: Artisans call their art telkari: silver filigree worked into tiny lace patterns, passed from master to apprentice for centuries in Midyat. Several workshops can be visited in the old town. Prices seem high, but the work is measured in hours, not grams. Look for the Turkish 925 hallmark to authenticate the silver.

practical_info.tip: Avoid tourist-trap shops near the Konukevi; go deeper into the alleys.

activities.text: Taste Syriac wine in a stone cellar: Midyat's Christian community has cultivated vines for centuries, and several cellars serve local vintages in 19th-century stone houses. The reds are full-bodied, the whites rarer. Expect 200 to 300 TL for a tasting with a platter.

practical_info.tip: Church cellar service is by reservation; ask your hotel.

visits.text: A 12,000-year-old town swallowed in a few months: the Ilısu Dam began flooding Hasankeyf in 2020. The 12th-century Artuqid bridge, the inhabited caves, the bazaar: everything is underwater now. What remains is a melancholy visit, almost an act of memory.

Relocated in 2017, the Zeynel Bey mausoleum is one of eight major monuments rescued from the dam and reassembled at the new cultural park of Yeni Hasankeyf, on a hill above the lake. The Persian tomb in blue and turquoise bricks of an Aq Qoyunlu prince is universally acclaimed. Small modern museum displays the relocated pieces.

activities.text: Climb up to Hasankeyf Citadel: spared by the waters because perched too high, it remains accessible and offers a heartbreaking view of the lake that covers the old town. Allow 30 minutes of climbing, steep but short. Bring water; no service at the top. The old cave dwellings still visible on the cliff side are worth a stop.

practical_info.tip: Free entry, but open 8am to 6pm only.

visits.text: Batman surprises: an oil town, flat, with no obvious charm, it's mainly a practical stop before Diyarbakır. Born in the 1940s with the discovery of oil, it only urbanized in the 20th century. Its archaeology museum deserves an hour for the pieces rescued from the Tigris valley before the Hasankeyf flood.

Dating from 1146-1147, the Malabadi Bridge spans the Batman Su with a single stone arch nearly 40 meters wide, one of the widest in the medieval world. Built by the Artuqids, it still serves as an arch for pedestrians. It's 30 km east of the city, on the road to Silvan, and can be visited for free.

activities.text: Eat a yoğurtlu leben, Batman-style yogurt soup thickened with fine bulgur and flavored with dried mint. Several lokantas in the center serve it at lunch, about 70 TL per bowl. It's the regional dish less known than Antep's beyran, but just as characteristic. Served with fresh flatbread.

practical_info.tip: Batman's center lunches between noon and 2pm; after that, lokantas empty their pots.

visits.text: UNESCO-listed in 2015, the black ramparts of Diyarbakır form a 5.8 km ring of volcanic basalt around the Sur district. It's one of the longest medieval enclosures still standing in the world. The ramparts date largely from the Byzantine era, 4th-6th centuries, with Roman and Islamic additions.

The basalt heats under your fingers, dark and pitted. The local volcanic rock is so present that the city was nicknamed Kara Amid (black Amida) until the 16th century. The ramparts count 82 bastions and four main gates (Harput, Mardin, Urfa, Yeni), from the Romans to the Ottomans. The Mardinkapı and Urfakapı gates are the best preserved.

Locals say Kara Amid, black Amida. The Sur district, within the walls, suffered from the 2015-2016 clashes; some blocks remain inaccessible or under reconstruction. Check before venturing into certain alleys. The tour along the top of the ramparts remains safe and marked, in good condition on the southern half.

activities.text: Walk 4 km on the rampart walkway on the Mardinkapı side: it's the best-preserved section for views over the Tigris and the Hevsel gardens below. Three hours on foot with photo stops. Access is from the Mardin gate, paid ticket at the entrance. Avoid the hot summer hours; no shade on the wall.

practical_info.tip: Access stairs are steep; not recommended for people with reduced mobility.

activities.text: If you come in spring, descend to the Hevsel gardens: 700 hectares of vegetable gardens irrigated by the Tigris, UNESCO-listed with the ramparts. Many bird species nest there, including herons and egrets. Marked trail from the Mardin gate, allow 1.5 hours round trip on foot.

practical_info.tip: The gardens are private but accessible to walkers; respect the crops.

map_keywords: Cahit Sıtkı Tarancı House Museum Diyarbakır

visits.text: The Ulu Camii beats the Umayyad Mosque of Damascus for age in Anatolia: it's considered the oldest great mosque still standing in Turkey. Its northern façade, with reused Corinthian columns and reliefs of a bull attacked by a lion, looks like no other. Women: scarf and covered legs mandatory.

Rebuilt in 1091 by the Seljuks, the Ulu Camii adopts the plan of the Umayyad mosque of Damascus, transposed into black basalt and white limestone. The adjoining Mesudiye Medresesi, completed in 1198 by the Artuqids, is one of the region's first theological schools. Black-and-white chevron decoration, very distinctive.

In the Sur bazaar, the smell of tütün and hot tobacco mingles with stalls of dried fruit and copper. The market stretches from the Ulu Camii to the Mardin gate, along Gazi Street. Less touristy than those of Urfa or Antep, more authentic. Look for Kurdish passementerie and black filigree jewelry, a city specialty.

activities.text: Follow Gazi Street to the Cahit Sıtkı Tarancı house, a Kurdish-Turkish poet born in Diyarbakır in 1910. His family home, a magnificent example of Sur's vernacular architecture in basalt and wood, now serves as a museum. Modest entry; allow 45 minutes. The black-and-white checkerboard inner courtyard is typical of the region.

practical_info.tip: Closed Mondays; photography prohibited inside.

activities.text: The Dengbêj are Kurdish storytellers: their house in Diyarbakır, opened in 2007 in Sur, hosts their traditional improvised songs, accompanied by tea. Sessions take place in the afternoon, free. You won't understand the lyrics, but the deep voice grain and oral rhythm are enough to tell a story.

practical_info.tip: Sessions vary; ask the guardian at the entrance.

seo.h1_title: Turkish Mesopotamia: 11 Days from Gaziantep to the Tigris
seo.intro_paragraph: 11 days to cross Southeast Anatolia, from the gastronomic capital of Gaziantep to the black ramparts of Diyarbakır. You'll follow the Euphrates at Halfeti, climb to the world's oldest known sanctuary at Göbekli Tepe, sleep in the honey-colored stone of Mardin, and descend to the Tigris in the sunken city of Hasankeyf.
seo.seo_hook: Göbekli Tepe, Gaziantep baklava, Mardin's Syriac monasteries, and UNESCO-listed ramparts of Diyarbakır: 11 days crossing Turkish Mesopotamia.
featured_list: Gaziantep: UNESCO City of Gastronomy, capital of pistachio baklava
Halfeti: old village submerged by the Birecik dam in 2000
Şanlıurfa: Balıklıgöl, Abraham's sacred pool, and museum of the world's oldest statue
Göbekli Tepe: Neolithic megalithic sanctuary, UNESCO-inscribed in 2018
Mardin: honey stone, Syriac monastery of Deyrulzafaran, terraces over the plain
Diyarbakır: 5.8 km of black basalt ramparts, UNESCO-listed in 2015

itineraries.title: 7-Day Taurus: Turquoise Lakes & Lycian Cities
itineraries.subtitle: In 7 days, journey from Antalya to Eğirdir, through Sagalassos and Lake Salda, ending in Fethiye.
itineraries.notes: Rose harvest in Isparta runs from mid-May through late June—the ideal period for this itinerary. Sagalassos and Lake Salda sit at altitude; evenings remain cool even in summer.
itineraries.climate: Best period: April-May and September-October, daytime temperatures 20-28°C. Avoid July-August (scorching heat, 35-40°C inland, archaeological sites unbearable at midday). Mountain lakes stay cool, possible frost in winter.

visits.text: Three white marble arches cut through the urban fabric of Kaleiçi: Hadrian's Gate, sole vestige of Antalya's Roman ramparts. Built in 130 AD for the emperor's visit. The coffered ceiling is still legible if you look up. Walk through the central arch—it's been the custom for 1,900 years.

The fluted Yivli Minare dates from the 13th century, erected under the Seljuk sultanate. Its red-brick silhouette with eight vertical grooves has become the city's emblem. The mosque at its base is still active. Exterior visit free; interior outside prayer times (headscarf for women).

Hıdırlık Tower has watched over the Roman harbour since the 2nd century AD, standing at the southwest corner of Kaleiçi. Likely a lighthouse or funerary monument originally, later repurposed as a fortification. The view plunges over Antalya Bay and the Taurus foothills, snow-capped in winter. Climb it at sunset.

activities.text: Head down to Antalya's old harbour in late afternoon for sunset. Fishing boats share the water with tourist caiques, quayside terraces serve chilled raki at reasonable prices off-season. Avoid restaurants during peak hours; count on 400 to 600 TL for an honest mezze-fish meal.

practical_info.tip: Skip restaurants with touts; walk two streets back instead.

activities.text: Touristy, but the Suna-İnan Kıraç Museum warrants an hour. Housed in a restored Greek Orthodox church and Ottoman mansion in Kaleiçi, it presents reconstructed scenes of Turkish daily life and Çanakkale ceramics. Entry around 50 TL, generally closed Wednesdays.

practical_info.tip: The garden with the Orthodox chapel makes a fine refuge from the heat.

visits.text: Termessos sent Alexander the Great packing in 333 BC. The conqueror dubbed the city an 'eagle's nest' before abandoning the siege. The Solymi, a Pisidian people, occupied this mountain stronghold at 1,050 m altitude on Mount Güllük (ancient Solymos, 1,665 m at the summit). The national park now encompasses the entire massif.

Termessos's theatre clings to the mountainside at 1,050 m, facing the Taurus peaks. 4,200 seats carved from limestone, a raw panorama over the range and the Pamphylian plain. Go early; fog often rolls in around 11 am. Sarcophagi lie scattered through the surrounding pine woods, some prised open by treasure hunters.

activities.text: Allow 4 hours and proper footwear at Termessos. The trail from the car park climbs 1 km with roughly 200 m elevation gain. No refreshments inside; water and a hat are mandatory in summer. National park entry is modest, separate site ticket (free with Museum Pass). Snakes possible; don't lift stones.

practical_info.tip: If you have time, the tomb of Alcetas is in the western necropolis.

visits.text: Eğirdir's Byzantine fortress is now just a wall and a gate, but it dominated the rocky bottleneck between lake and mountain for centuries. Built initially around 400 BC according to local guides (take the date with caution), rebuilt by the Seljuks. The view over the lake from the summit redeems the site's austerity.

Hızır Bey Mosque and Dündar Bey Medresesi face each other in the centre of Eğirdir, both from the early 1200s. The medrese, restored, sometimes hosts a craft market beneath its vaults. Pale stone, Seljuk portal with muqarnas. Free visit; headscarf for the mosque.

Yeşilada stretches at the end of a land bridge extending the town 1 km into the lake. It's a former Greek island linked to the mainland by an embankment, still dotted with stone houses from the 1900s. Walk along both shores: calm water on one side, ruffled by wind on the other—two microclimates across 30 metres.

activities.text: Locals call Eğirdir 'little Switzerland' for its Akpınar mountains ringing the lake. Rent a mountain bike at Anatoly Bisiklet Evi (around 200 TL per day) and loop the peninsula. The Saint Paul Trail passes through here; red-white blazes visible from the centre.

practical_info.tip: The lake water stays cool even in summer, rarely above 23-24°C.

activities.text: Sample Eğirdir apples in September-October: the region is one of Turkey's major orchards, with pyramids of apples sold roadside on the town's outskirts. Lake fish (pike-perch, pike) also feature on every menu. Arzava Restaurant serves an honest version for 300-400 TL.

practical_info.tip: Local apples keep well; grab a bag for the rest of your trip.

visits.text: Isparta smells of roses the moment you step out of the car, especially in May-June. The province cultivates Rosa damascena for the global perfume trade and reportedly produces around 65% of the world's rose oil, according to official figures. Harvest is artisanal, by hand, at dawn when the flower is full of oil.

Isparta Museum houses carpets and kilims, testament to the town's textile heritage, along with Bronze Age artefacts. Also visit the 1561 Firdevs Paşa Mosque and the Atabey Ertokuş Medresesi, one of the oldest Seljuk structures in the region. Compact cluster; allow 2 hours on foot.

activities.text: If you're passing between mid-May and late June, head to Güneykent or Güneyköy 30 km southwest to join a dawn harvest. Several family distilleries offer visits with tastings. Count on 200 to 400 TL for a guided morning. It takes roughly 4 tonnes of petals to produce 1 kg of pure oil.

practical_info.tip: You'll leave smelling of roses all day; bring a top you can wash.

visits.text: Virtually no one in the Sagalassos ruins on a Tuesday morning in September—one of the site's great pleasures. This Pisidian city perched on Mount Akdağ around 1,500 m was abandoned around the mid-7th century after several earthquakes. Belgian excavations since 1989 (Marc Waelkens); inscribed on UNESCO's Tentative List.

The Antonine Fountain, restored in 2010, flows again for the first time in roughly 1,500 years. Built under Marcus Aurelius around 160-180 AD, it lines the full length of the upper agora. Statues replaced by copies (originals in Burdur Museum). The theatre, at 1,500 m, is one of the world's highest from antiquity.

activities.text: Park at the Sagalassos lot after 7 km of switchbacks from Ağlasun; allow 3 hours on site. The site is terraced, the fountain stands at the top. Water and cap essential; little shade. Goats graze among the columns—don't approach too closely. Picnicking permitted outside the excavation zone.

practical_info.tip: Burdur Museum downstream displays the colossal head of Hadrian found here.

visits.text: Surprising for such a modest town: Burdur Museum houses the colossal head of Hadrian recovered at Sagalassos by Marc Waelkens, one of the finest known representations of the emperor. The dancer statues from the Sagalassos Heroon are also exhibited here, better preserved than the on-site copies. Allow 1.5 hours; closed Mondays.

İnsuyu Cave, 13 km east of Burdur, was the first cave opened to tourism in Turkey. Stalactites, stalagmites, a small underground lake. Guided tour around 30 minutes; stairs are damp and slippery. Water level varies with rainfall, sometimes closed during droughts. Check before you go.

activities.text: Go birdwatching at Lake Burdur, a Ramsar site since 1994. The lake has lost over a third of its water in 50 years; current surface area roughly 150 km². The white-headed duck (Oxyura leucocephala), globally threatened, nests here. Bring binoculars; observation best in autumn-winter.

practical_info.tip: The north shore is more accessible than the south; several viewing platforms.

visits.text: Lake Salda unfurls its unreal turquoise at the foot of Eşeler Dağı. Alkaline waters (pH around 9), depths to 196 m, white hydromagnesite beaches. One of Turkey's deepest crater lakes. Protected area since 1989, designated a special environmental protection zone in 2019.

NASA studies Salda as a terrestrial analogue of Jezero Crater on Mars, where the Perseverance rover has been searching for traces of ancient life since 2021. The hydromagnesite microbialites resemble the carbonates detected at Jezero. The space agency has published comparative images on its official site.

activities.text: Only swim in Lake Salda's designated areas now. Since 2021, several stretches of shore have been off-limits to preserve the microbialites and white sand. Doğanbaba beach remains open, easy access from Yeşilova. Sandals essential; the sand is compact but sharp in places. Don't remove sand.

practical_info.tip: Sunset spectacular from the east shore, quiet on weekdays.

visits.text: The Tomb of Amyntas has loomed over Fethiye since the 4th century BC, carved as an Ionic temple façade into the limestone cliff. It's the most imposing of the Lycian tombs from ancient Telmessos. Count roughly 200 steps from Fethiye's Kaleiçi, steep ascent. Entry modest. Go before 9 am or after 5 pm for the light on the façade.

Paspatur Bazaar exhales spices and leather through the alleyways of old Fethiye. Stone houses rebuilt after the 1957 earthquake, an atmosphere mixing local fishermen and yachtsmen. Sailors' market on Tuesdays, fruit and vegetable market on Fridays. More authentic than the package-tour markets of Ölüdeniz.

Kayaköy is now just a shell: a Greek village abandoned in 1923 during the population exchange between Greece and Turkey, roughly 500 empty stone houses, two roofless churches. 8 km southeast of Fethiye. Entry modest; allow 2 hours to walk the lanes. Eerie atmosphere, especially late afternoon.

Ölüdeniz, the blue lagoon of the Lycian coast, lies 15 km south of Fethiye. Public beach (Belcekız) and protected lagoon (paid entry), translucent water among the pines. The resort is heavily built-up but the lagoon remains superb. Paragliding possible from Babadağ at 1,969 m, directly overhead. Diving best avoided, sadly saturated.

activities.text: Walk the first stretch of the Lycian Way, a 535 km long-distance trail marked in red and white that officially starts at Ovacık, near Fethiye. The Fethiye-Kayaköy stage (around 8 km, 4-5 hours) passes above the tombs and descends to the ghost village. Hiking boots and water essential.

practical_info.tip: You can shorten it by taking a dolmuş for the second half.

activities.text: Paragliding from Babadağ is touristy but exhilarating: take-off at 1,969 m, landing on Ölüdeniz beach, tandem flight 30 to 45 minutes depending on thermals. Rates around €80 to €120, photos and videos included with reputable operators. Choose one accredited by the Turkish Aerosport Federation; Babadağ has its share of accidents.

practical_info.tip: Morning flight calmer, afternoon flight more turbulent but more aerial.

seo.intro_paragraph: 7 days in the Western Taurus, between the Mediterranean and high plateaux. Climb from Antalya to Eğirdir and Sagalassos, cross Isparta's rose fields, plunge into Lake Salda, and descend to Fethiye via Kayaköy. Slow travel and easy hiking.
seo.seo_hook: Termessos perched at 1,050 m, Sagalassos, turquoise Lake Salda, and Fethiye's Lycian tombs: 7 days in the Western Taurus, away from the beaches.

Sagalassos and its Antonine Fountain, restored in 2010
Lake Salda, terrestrial analogue of Mars's Jezero Crater per NASA
